planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade beneath conifer canopy or along a streambank; this rush spreads slowly and is propagated almost entirely by division rather than seed.

directions: Small-flowered woodrush forms modest, grass-like tufts of flat, hair-fringed blades that stay green through the cool, wet months typical of Olympic Peninsula old-growth forest floors and streamside benches. Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in shade to partial shade, where the fibrous roots can knit into duff without competing against aggressive groundcovers. Loose, open sprays of small brown-bronze flower clusters nod above the foliage in summer on wiry stems, adding a fine textural accent rather than a showy bloom. Established clumps need steady moisture and tolerate deep shade well, making this woodrush a useful quiet filler at the base of conifers or along a shaded streambank planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container starts in spring into woodland soil in partial to full shade at a Douglas-fir or oak-forest edge, watering regularly through the first season to establish the fibrous root system.

directions: Henderson's sedge forms an arching, fountain-like clump of pleated, dark green evergreen blades that holds its shape through the wet Pacific Northwest winter and the dry forest-floor summer alike. Plant divisions or container starts in spring into woodland soil at the edge of Douglas-fir or oak canopy, in partial to full shade, watering regularly the first season while roots establish. Thin, inconspicuous green flowering spikes rise just above the foliage in spring, giving way quietly to the sedge's main appeal, its graceful year-round form. Once rooted, established clumps tolerate surprisingly dry shade and need little supplemental water, making this an easy substitute for turf or a textural accent beneath native shade trees.

planting.note: Direct-sow seed or set out plugs in fall into lean, well-drained woodland soil in partial shade to light shade at a forest edge or opening; winter rains settle the fine roots before the first dry season.

directions: Western fescue grows as a fine-bladed, gently arching bunchgrass naturally found at the dappled edges and openings of Pacific Northwest conifer forest, rather than in open prairie like most native fescues. Sow seed in fall or set out plugs into lean, well-drained woodland soil in partial shade to light shade, where winter rain will settle the fibrous roots before the first dry season. Slender, nodding flower panicles rise above the narrow basal foliage in late spring, adding airy movement without the need for staking. Once established the clumps are drought tolerant and persist for years without division, making this fescue a low-maintenance textural companion for ferns and other shade-tolerant natives at a woodland garden's edge.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in fall into well-drained, humus-amended soil in partial shade against a rock outcrop or canyon wall, or beneath open tree canopy, so winter rain can settle the roots before spring bloom.

directions: Island alumroot forms a substantial, long-lived mound of broad, lobed, leathery evergreen leaves that cling to shaded canyon walls and rocky slopes on the northern Channel Islands, far larger in scale than most mainland alumroots. Plant divisions or container stock in fall into well-drained, humus-amended soil in partial shade, siting it against a rock outcrop, canyon wall, or beneath open tree canopy where its roots can wedge into crevices. Tall, airy flower stalks rise well above the foliage from late winter into spring, carrying small cream to pale pink bells that draw native bees and occasional hummingbirds. Once established it needs only light supplemental water, tolerating both the coastal fog of its island habitat and considerably drier, shadier mainland garden settings.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall into well-drained soil on a canyon-like slope with some overhead shelter or light shade from taller companions, mimicking the partially sheltered island canyons where this species survives wild.

directions: Catalina ceanothus is the largest-growing of California's native ceanothus species, forming a dense, rounded evergreen shrub or small multi-trunked tree with glossy, deeply veined leaves felted gray-green beneath, native only to a handful of Channel Island canyon groves. Plant container stock in fall into well-drained soil, choosing a canyon-like site with some shelter from the hottest afternoon sun or light shade from taller companions, since island populations often grow under a partial canopy rather than in fully exposed chaparral. Large, soft blue to pale lavender flower clusters smother the branches in spring, drawing heavy bee and butterfly activity over several weeks. Once its roots are established the shrub needs little summer water and resents heavy or frequently irrigated soils, making a lightly shaded, well-drained slope its best long-term home.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring into well-drained soil in full coastal sun or a half-day of shade; this fast-growing island shrub quickly fills in and tolerates more shade than most of its coastal-bluff relatives.

directions: Island mallow is a fast-growing, woody-based Channel Islands endemic that can reach small-tree proportions within just a few seasons, bearing large, soft maple-like leaves and an extended succession of showy, lavender-pink, hibiscus-style flowers from spring through summer. Plant container stock in spring into well-drained soil in a site that gets full coastal sun or a half-day of shade, since this species tolerates considerably more shade than most of its coastal-bluff neighbors. Its rapid growth and dense branching make it a quick privacy screen or specimen shrub, and the long bloom season is a reliable draw for bees and hummingbirds. Prune lightly after the main flowering flush to control its naturally sprawling habit, and avoid overwatering once established, since the species evolved on exposed island bluffs with lean, fast-draining soil.
